title: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages: Equivalence and Ordering
kicker: Checkpoint 6 Maths · Number · Fractions, decimals and percentages
summary: Change confidently between fractions, decimals and percentages, find percentages of shapes and amounts, and compare and order mixed numbers with =, > and <.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Know that a fraction, a decimal (with one or two decimal places) and a percentage can have the same value, e.g. 3/4 = 0.75 = 75% (6Nf.04)
Recognise percentages of shapes and of whole numbers: 1% and multiples of 5% up to 100%, e.g. 35% of a shape, 15% of 60 (6Nf.07)
Compare and order decimals (one or two decimal places), proper fractions with different denominators and percentages, using =, > and < (6Nf.08)

blocks.text: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three different ways of writing the **same** amount. Half a pizza is 1/2, 0.5 or 50% of it. If you can move quickly between the three forms, you can compare any two numbers, find percentages of amounts in your head and answer a lot of Checkpoint questions in seconds.
Key words

items: per cent (%)
في المئة — 'out of 100'; 35% means 35 out of 100
percentage
النسبة المئوية — an amount written out of 100 with the % sign
decimal
عدد عشري — a number with a decimal point, e.g. 0.35
tenth / hundredth
جزء من عشرة / جزء من مئة — 0.1 = 1/10, 0.01 = 1/100
equivalent
مكافئ / متساوي في القيمة — worth the same, e.g. 1/4 and 25%
simplest form
أبسط صورة — e.g. 35/100 simplified to 7/20
common denominator
مقام مشترك — the same denominator for two fractions so you can compare them
greater than >, less than <
أكبر من، أصغر من — the open side of the sign faces the bigger number
ascending order
ترتيب تصاعدي — from smallest to largest

blocks.text: 1. What does 'per cent' mean?

**Per cent means 'out of 100'.** If a square is cut into 100 equal small squares and 35 are shaded, then 35/100 of it is shaded. That is 35 hundredths, which as a decimal is 0.35, and as a percentage is 35%.

blocks.text: 2. Changing between the three forms

rows: make the denominator 100 with an equivalent fraction
make the denominator 10 or 100, or divide numerator ÷ denominator
use place value (tenths or hundredths), then simplify

blocks.title: Making the denominator 100
blocks.text: Ask: 'What do I multiply the denominator by to get 100?' Then multiply the numerator by the same number. Denominators that work easily: 2 (× 50), 4 (× 25), 5 (× 20), 10 (× 10), 20 (× 5), 25 (× 4), 50 (× 2). Example: 9/25 → × 4 → 36/100 = 0.36 = 36%.

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية
blocks.text: النسبة المئوية يعني "من 100". علشان تحوّل كسر لنسبة مئوية خلّي المقام 100: مثلاً 7/20 = 35/100 = 35%. ومن عشري لنسبة مئوية اضرب في 100: 0.6 = 60% (مش 6%). ومن نسبة مئوية لعشري اقسم على 100: 5% = 0.05.
3. Percentages of shapes

To find what percentage of a shape is shaded, the shape must be split into **equal** parts. Work out what percentage **one** part is (100% ÷ the number of parts), then multiply by the number of shaded parts.

blocks.text: You can also go the other way: 'Shade 35% of a shape with 20 squares.' Each square is 5%, and 35% ÷ 5% = 7, so shade **7 squares**.
4. Percentages of whole numbers
Build every percentage from a few easy ones. You never need a calculator for 1% or multiples of 5%.

blocks.text: 5. Comparing and ordering
To compare numbers written in different forms, **change them all into the same form** — usually decimals with two decimal places, or percentages. Then compare digit by digit from the left.

items: Change every number to a decimal with **two** decimal places (write 0.6 as 0.60).
Compare the tenths first, then the hundredths.
Put them in order, then write the **original** numbers (not your decimals) in the answer.
For two fractions, you can also use a **common denominator**: 3/4 and 7/10 → 15/20 and 14/20, so 3/4 > 7/10.

blocks.title: The signs =, > and <
blocks.text: The wide open side of the sign faces the bigger number: 0.75 > 0.7 (0.75 is greater than 0.7), 0.09 < 0.1 (0.09 is less than 0.1). Use = only when the values are exactly the same, e.g. 2/5 = 40%.
6. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Write 0.35 (a) as a fraction in its simplest form (b) as a percentage. [2]
(a) 0.35 = 35 hundredths = 35/100. The HCF of 35 and 100 is 5: 35/100 = **7/20**. (b) 0.35 × 100 = **35%**. Common mistake: writing 35/10 or 3.5%.
**Worked example 2** — A shape is made of 20 equal squares. 9 are shaded. What percentage is shaded? [1]
**Worked example 3** — Find 35% of 80. [1]
**Worked example 4** — Find (a) 1% of 600 (b) 95% of 600. [2]

(a) 600 ÷ 100 = **6**. (b) 95% = 100% − 5%. 10% of 600 = 60, so 5% = 30. 600 − 30 = **570**. Common mistake: finding 95% as 9 × 10% + 5% and adding wrongly — subtracting from 100% is quicker and safer.
**Worked example 5** — Write >, < or = in each box. [2]   (a) 3/4 ☐ 0.7   (b) 2/5 ☐ 40%   (c) 0.09 ☐ 0.1

items: (c) 0.09 has 0 tenths; 0.1 = 0.10 has 1 tenth. So **0.09 < 0.1**. Common mistake: thinking 0.09 is bigger because 9 > 1.
Mark scheme style: 2 marks for all three correct, 1 mark for two correct.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Which is bigger, 5/8 or 7/12? Show how you know. [1]
Find a common denominator: 24 is a multiple of both 8 and 12. 5/8 = 15/24 (× 3) and 7/12 = 14/24 (× 2). 15/24 > 14/24, so **5/8 is bigger** (see the fraction bars above).
**Worked example 7** — Write these numbers in order, starting with the smallest: 0.62   3/5   66%   0.58   16/25 [2]
Order of the decimals: 0.58, 0.60, 0.62, 0.64, 0.66. **Answer: 0.58, 3/5, 0.62, 16/25, 66%.** Write the numbers as they were given, not the decimals.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: 'Longer decimals are bigger': 0.56 is NOT bigger than 0.6. Write 0.6 as 0.60 and compare tenths first.
Comparing fractions by the denominator only: 1/8 looks 'bigger' because 8 > 4, but 1/8 < 1/4.
Counting shaded parts of a shape that is not split into equal parts, or forgetting how many parts the whole has.
In ordering questions, writing the converted decimals instead of the original numbers, or ordering largest first when the question says smallest first.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: Matching lines: join each fraction to the equal decimal or percentage.
Complete a table of equivalent fractions, decimals and percentages.
'What percentage of the shape is shaded?' or 'Shade 45% of this shape' on a grid.
Find a percentage of an amount (often money or pupils), e.g. 15% of $60 — show 10% and 5% in your working.
Write >, < or = in a box, ring the largest/smallest, or order a mixed list. Change everything into decimals or percentages first and write your conversions next to the numbers.
'Explain how you know' — show the common denominator or the conversions; a bare answer may not get the mark.

questions.q: What percentage of the shape is shaded?
questions.e: Count the shaded squares: 5 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 13. Each square is 100% ÷ 20 = 5%. 13 × 5% = **65%**. (Or 13/20 = 65/100.)

questions.e: 0.6 = 0.60 > 0.56, so A is wrong. 0.5 = 50% and 50% > 45%, so **B is correct**. 7/10 = 70% > 65%, so C is wrong. 1/4 = 0.25 < 0.3, so D is wrong.
Change all to decimals: 0.72, 0.70, 0.07, 0.75. The largest is 0.75 = **3/4**.

questions.e: As decimals: A = 0.35, B = 0.30, C = 0.33, D = 0.40. Smallest to largest: 0.30, 0.33, 0.35, 0.40 → **B C A D**. (1 mark if one pair is in the wrong order.)

questions.q: Which is bigger, 2/3 or 5/8? Show how you know.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a correct method — both fractions written with a common denominator (e.g. 16/24 and 15/24) or correctly drawn equal-length fraction bars, or both written as close decimals (0.66… and 0.625). 1 mark: 2/3 is bigger, from correct working. Do not award the second mark for '2/3' with no working.

questions.p:
Question 13
A school has 400 pupils. 45% of the pupils walk to school. 25% of the pupils come by bus.
questions.q: (a) How many pupils walk to school?

questions.p:
Question 13
A school has 400 pupils. 45% of the pupils walk to school. 25% of the pupils come by bus.
questions.q: (b) How many more pupils walk than come by bus?
questions.e: 25% of 400 = 400 ÷ 4 = 100 come by bus. 180 − 100 = **80**. (Quicker: 45% − 25% = 20%, and 20% of 400 = 80.) Follow through from (a).

blocks.title: Remember
items: Per cent means out of 100: 35% = 35/100 = 0.35.
Percentages of amounts: build from 10% (÷ 10), 5% (half of 10%), 1% (÷ 100), 50% and 25%.
Percentage of a shape: 100% ÷ number of equal parts = value of one part.
To compare or order, change everything to the same form (two-decimal-place decimals or percentages), then compare tenths first.
